title: Tamannaah Bhatia Just Said Out Loud What South Cinema's Actresses Whisper: "It's a Gaze That's Not Very Complimenting"
excerpt: Two decades, three industries, and one very candid Forbes India sit-down. The Baahubali star drew a line between Bollywood's open lane and the South's stricter glare — and refused to call her dance numbers 'item songs.'
body:
There's a particular kind of courage it takes for a woman who has spent twenty years inside an industry to turn around and describe exactly how it looked at her. **Tamannaah Bhatia** found it this week.

In an interview with *Forbes India*, the actress — who has moved fluidly between Telugu, Tamil and Hindi sets since she was a teenager — was asked about the difference between Bollywood and the South. She didn't reach for the diplomatic answer. "It's a very specific gaze," she said of South commercial cinema. "It's a patriarchal sort of vibe, or it's a gaze that's not very complimenting."

> "The South needed that star quality to be able to pull that off. I personally feel that cinema is as restrictive, or even more restrictive, in that sense — when you want to make it from a commercial standpoint." — Tamannaah Bhatia, to Forbes India

It is the sort of line that detonates quietly and then keeps going off for days. Coming from anyone else it might read as sour grapes. Coming from Tamannaah — a woman who *made it* in exactly that system, who carried **Baahubali**'s Avantika and a hundred mass-hero entries on her shoulders — it reads as testimony.

What makes the quote land is that she isn't burning the house down. She's measuring it. Bollywood, in her telling, runs two lanes: the actor with "a more artistic take" who skips the glamorous song-and-dance, and the one who does it all. "The Hindi film industry actually gives you the opportunity to do either/or," she said, "and the ones who do both inevitably become superstars." The South, she suggested, narrows that road to one — be the goddess, hit the beat, hold the frame, or step aside.

And here's the twist that keeps this from being a tidy feminist headline: Tamannaah refuses to be embarrassed by the glamour itself. She will not call her hits "item songs."

> "You might not remember those movies, but you will always remember a 'Chammak Challo', a 'Sheila Ki Jawani' or a 'Kamli'. You remember these songs that these wonderful women have done. They look like goddesses, they move like goddesses. They are beauty personified." — Tamannaah Bhatia

It's a genuinely interesting position, and a slippery one. She's holding two truths at once: that the gaze trained on Southern heroines can be reductive *and* that the dance number — performed on a woman's own terms — is an act of power, not surrender. "I don't look at it like an item," she said, "because I feel these eventually become party songs." The frame at the wedding sangeet, the aunty and the teenager dancing to the same hook twenty years apart — that, to her, is the legacy, not the runtime of the film it came from.

There's a lovely, very human footnote buried in the interview, too: when the days get hard, Tamannaah and her team put on **Himesh Reshammiya** and dance it out. Make of that what you will. We find it perfect.


The diaspora context here is sharper than it looks. For NRI audiences in the US, UK and Canada — who increasingly watch Telugu and Tamil blockbusters in packed multiplexes the same weekend they release back home, and who stream them dubbed on **Netflix**, **Prime Video** and **JioHotstar** — the South is no longer the 'other' cinema. It's the dominant export. Pan-India is the business model now. So when one of its most recognisable faces says the camera's gaze on its women is "not very complimenting," that's not gossip. It's a note about the product half the diaspora is consuming on a Friday night.

It won't be the last word. Gulte, the Telugu trade outlet, framed it bluntly — "Tamannah takes a dig at the South industry yet again" — a reminder that she's said versions of this before and been told to be grateful. That's rather the point. The actresses who built these industries are starting to narrate them, out loud, with their names attached.

Whether the South listens is another matter. But Avantika just handed every young heroine walking onto a commercial set a sentence to carry in her back pocket. "It's a gaze that's not very complimenting." Now somebody's finally said it.
